title: Iran votes for an Islamic constitution while Americans stay hostage in Tehran
what: On 2 and 3 December Iranians approved a new constitution that makes the country an Islamic republic led by a senior cleric; the official result was 99.5 percent yes, though leftists, secular nationalists, followers of Ayatollah Shariatmadari and the Mojahedin boycotted the vote. In Tehran, students who stormed the US embassy on 4 November still hold 53 Americans, after freeing 13 women and African Americans in November. Washington stopped buying Iranian oil on 12 November and froze about 8 billion dollars of Iranian assets on 14 November. Gold ended the month above 500 dollars an ounce.
why: Opens the arc: the revolution's first winter, a new state built around Khomeini and a standoff with America that sets the tone for forty years. The hostage crisis, the oil cut-off and (late in the month) the Soviet entry into Afghanistan together drove gold's December jump; the hostages are only part of it.

title: America breaks with Iran, and a rescue mission dies in the desert
what: On 7 April the United States cut diplomatic relations with Iran and widened its sanctions. On 24 and 25 April a secret mission to free the hostages, Operation Eagle Claw, was called off in the Iranian desert; a helicopter then collided with a transport plane, killing eight American servicemen, and an Iranian civilian also died. Secretary of State Cyrus Vance resigned.
why: The low point of the crisis for Washington, and the moment the US-Iran break became permanent: there have been no diplomatic relations since.

title: Iraq invades Iran
what: On 22 September Iraqi aircraft struck ten Iranian airfields, and the next day Iraqi troops crossed the border along a front of more than 600 kilometres, aiming above all at the oil province of Khuzestan and the Shatt al-Arab waterway. Saddam Hussein had torn up the 1975 border agreement with Iran days before. Iran, its army purged after the revolution, is fighting back with regular troops, Revolutionary Guards and volunteers. Oil output from both countries is disrupted.
why: Begins the eight-year war that Iranians call the 'imposed war' or the 'sacred defence', which killed hundreds of thousands and shaped a generation. The war took further oil off the market (about 7 percent of world output by one estimate), which belongs to the oil arc.

title: The hostages fly home after 444 days
what: Under the Algiers Accords signed on 19 January, with Algeria as go-between, Iran released the 52 remaining American hostages on 20 January, minutes after Ronald Reagan was sworn in. In return, Iranian gold and securities frozen in the United States are being released through the Algerian central bank, and a tribunal in The Hague will settle claims between the two countries. The hostages were held for 444 days.
why: Ends the crisis that defined Carter's last year and opens the long, cold US-Iran relationship. The Iran-US Claims Tribunal it created still exists.

title: Iran's president deposed, then a bomb kills Beheshti and dozens of leaders
what: On 21 June parliament voted to remove President Abolhassan Banisadr, Iran's first elected president, and Khomeini signed his dismissal the next day; a rally for him on 20 June ended with about 50 dead and hundreds arrested. On 28 June a bomb at the Islamic Republican Party headquarters in Tehran killed Chief Justice Ayatollah Beheshti, four ministers, 27 members of parliament and many others, more than 70 people in all. The authorities blame the Mojahedin-e Khalq. Banisadr is in hiding.
why: The revolution turns on its own: what follows is a wave of arrests and executions of the left opposition, and another bombing killed the new president and prime minister on 30 August. Banisadr fled to France on 29 June. Who planted the June bomb is still disputed (the MEK never confirmed it, and Iran later blamed others), so the beat says 'blame'.

title: Iran retakes Khorramshahr
what: Iranian forces recaptured Khorramshahr on 24 May after a month-long offensive and say they took 15,000 to 19,000 Iraqi prisoners. Most Iraqi troops have now been pushed out of southern Iran.
why: The high point of Iran's war and the moment it could have ended; instead Iran crossed into Iraq in July (Operation Ramadan) and six more years of war followed. Khorramshahr had fallen to Iraq in late October or November 1980 after weeks of street fighting; Iranians called it Khuninshahr, the 'city of blood'.

title: Israel invades Lebanon
what: Israeli forces invaded Lebanon on 6 June with about 60,000 troops and more than 800 tanks, saying they would push PLO fighters 40 kilometres back from the border. By the end of the month they stood at the edge of Beirut, surrounding PLO and Syrian forces in the west of the city.
why: Starts the Lebanon thread: the siege of Beirut, the massacre at Sabra and Shatila, the Western peacekeepers and the birth of Hezbollah with Iranian help, which leads to the 2006 war and the 2024 strikes.

title: Battle of the marshes, and Iraq turns to poison gas
what: On 14 February Iranian forces seized the oil-rich Majnoon Islands in the marshes north of Basra, and fighting there went on into March with very heavy losses. Iraq has used mustard gas and, Iran says, nerve gas against Iranian troops; thousands of Iranian soldiers were affected in the marshes. Iraqi aircraft and missiles have also hit Iranian cities in February.
why: The war of attrition at its most brutal: human-wave offensives (Basij volunteers as young as 12 served) met with chemical weapons, the first verified battlefield use of nerve agent. The world largely looked away. Exact casualty figures from the marshes are estimates only (Iran about 50,000 casualties over the whole battle).

title: US warships escort Kuwaiti tankers; the UN demands a ceasefire
what: The US Navy began escorting Kuwaiti tankers re-registered under the American flag through the Gulf, and on 24 July the first convoy's tanker Bridgeton struck a mine. On 20 July the UN Security Council unanimously passed Resolution 598 demanding an immediate ceasefire between Iran and Iraq; Iraq accepted, Iran has not. On 31 July a clash between Iranian pilgrims and Saudi police in Mecca left 402 dead, 275 of them Iranians, by Saudi count; Iran says the police opened fire.
why: The tanker war (some 450 attacks on merchant ships, two-thirds by Iraq) brings America into direct confrontation with Iran. Resolution 598 is the text Iran finally accepted a year later. Who started the Mecca violence is disputed; Saudi Arabia cut relations in 1988. Iran had taken Iraq's Faw peninsula in February 1986, alarming Kuwait; in April 1988 Iraq retook Faw and the US Navy sank Iranian ships after a mine hit the USS Samuel B. Roberts, the turn that pushed Iran to accept 598.

title: Missiles on Tehran, poison gas on Halabja
what: Iraq has been firing long-range missiles at Tehran and other cities in a new 'war of the cities'. On 16 March Iraqi aircraft dropped chemical weapons on the Kurdish town of Halabja, which Iranian forces had just entered. Journalists brought in by Iran found streets of dead families; Iran says thousands of civilians were killed. Western reaction has been muted.
why: The war's cruellest month for civilians. Halabja's toll is usually given as 3,200 to 5,000; in the 1988 missile campaign Tehran was hit by 118 missiles over 52 days, killing about 420. Photographer Kaveh Golestan's pictures made Halabja known.

title: Khomeini accepts a ceasefire: 'more deadly than poison'
what: Iran said in mid-July that it accepts Resolution 598 and a ceasefire with Iraq. Ayatollah Khomeini said that accepting it was 'more deadly than drinking from a poisoned chalice'. UN observers are to supervise the truce. The war has lasted almost eight years; the dead are counted in the hundreds of thousands.
why: The end of the war. The ceasefire took effect on 20 August; no peace treaty was ever signed. In the weeks after, thousands of political prisoners were executed in secret, which the outside world learned of only slowly (see the .md).

title: Khomeini dies; Khamenei becomes Supreme Leader
what: Ayatollah Ruhollah Khomeini, leader of the revolution, died on 3 June aged 86. On 4 June the Assembly of Experts chose President Ali Khamenei as the new Supreme Leader. Millions of mourners filled Tehran for the funeral; in the crush people died and the body fell from its coffin, and a second ceremony had to be held.
why: The end of the founding era. Khamenei ruled for almost 37 years until he was killed in the 2026 war, which closes the arc. Rafsanjani, elected president in July with 94.5 percent (only two candidates approved), led the reconstruction years.

title: Earthquake devastates Gilan and Zanjan
what: A magnitude 7.4 earthquake struck northern Iran near the Caspian Sea in the early hours of 21 June, while most people slept in mud-brick houses. Tens of thousands are dead and hundreds of thousands homeless in the towns of Manjil and Rudbar and the villages around them. Iran has accepted aid from abroad, including from countries with which it has tense relations.
why: Iran's deadliest natural disaster of the era (final estimates 35,000 to 50,000 dead), two years after the war. The figure was still rising in late June, so 'what' says tens of thousands.

title: Desert Storm begins; oil falls by a third and stocks leap
what: After the UN's deadline of 15 January for Iraq to leave Kuwait passed, a US-led coalition of more than 40 countries began bombing Iraq and Iraqi forces in Kuwait on 17 January. Iraq has fired Scud missiles at Israel and Saudi Arabia. On the first day of the air war the oil price fell by about a third and the S&P 500 rose 3.7 percent.
why: A textbook case of 'sell the rumour, buy the war': the uncertainty was worse for markets than the fighting. Gives the game a clear month where war news lifted shares. The ground war of 24 to 28 February freed Kuwait, and the rally continued in February (S&P 500 +7%); retreating Iraqi troops set more than 600 Kuwaiti oil wells on fire.

title: Yitzhak Rabin assassinated at a peace rally
what: Israeli Prime Minister Yitzhak Rabin was shot dead on 4 November in Tel Aviv as he left a rally for the peace process attended by more than 100,000 people. The killer, Yigal Amir, is a 25-year-old Israeli law student opposed to the Oslo Accords. Shimon Peres has taken over.
why: The peace process never recovered its momentum.

title: Police storm Tehran University dormitories; students protest for days
what: After students protested on 8 July against the closing of the reformist newspaper Salam, police and plainclothes militiamen raided a Tehran University dormitory before dawn on 9 July, beating students and setting rooms on fire; at least one student was killed. Protests spread over the following days, with tens of thousands of students in Tehran and other cities, before they were put down and many were arrested.
why: '18 Tir', the first mass uprising of the generation born under the Islamic Republic, and the moment the limits of Khatami's reforms showed.

title: Attacks on New York and Washington; Wall Street's worst week since the 1930s
what: On 11 September hijackers flew airliners into the World Trade Center and the Pentagon, and a fourth plane crashed in Pennsylvania; thousands are dead or missing. US stock markets stayed shut until 17 September, when the Dow fell 684 points, 7.1 percent, its biggest one-day point loss, and ended the week down more than 14 percent; airline and insurance shares were hit hardest. In Tehran, people held candlelight vigils for the victims, and President Khatami sent his sympathy.
why: The defining event of the decade, leading to the wars in Afghanistan and Iraq. The Iranian vigils, unusual in the region, are part of the Iran story. Boeing's own fall that month belongs to its arc. Months of quiet US-Iranian cooperation against the Taliban followed, ended by Bush's 'axis of evil' speech of 29 January 2002.

title: Exiles reveal secret nuclear sites at Natanz and Arak
what: In August an Iranian exile opposition group made public the existence of two undeclared nuclear sites in Iran: a uranium enrichment plant at Natanz and a heavy-water facility at Arak. Iran says its programme is for electricity only. The International Atomic Energy Agency wants to inspect.
why: Starts the nuclear dispute that dominates the next 24 years of the arc, through sanctions, the 2015 deal and the strikes of 2025 and 2026.

title: The US and Britain invade Iraq
what: After President Bush's ultimatum to Saddam Hussein expired, US-led forces invaded Iraq on 20 March, with British, Australian and Polish troops. The stated aim is to disarm Iraq of weapons of mass destruction, which UN inspectors had not found, and remove Saddam. France, Germany and Canada opposed the war.
why: The war that remade the region and, by removing Iran's worst enemy, greatly widened Iran's influence in Iraq. No weapons of mass destruction were found.

title: Baghdad falls, and markets rally
what: US troops took Baghdad on 9 April, three weeks into the war. Iraqi oil fields were secured largely intact and the regime collapsed faster than feared. Oil prices have dropped and share prices have risen sharply.
why: The relief rally: markets had priced in a long war and fires in the oil fields. Studies of the period find shares rose as the war went well and the 'war premium' faded.

title: Earthquake destroys the city of Bam
what: At dawn on 26 December an earthquake flattened the city of Bam in southeastern Iran, most of whose houses were built of mud brick. By the end of the month more than 25,000 bodies had been recovered and estimates of the dead ran as high as 40,000. The ancient citadel, Arg-e Bam, is largely destroyed. Rescue teams from dozens of countries arrived; the United States, which has no relations with Iran, sent aid and a rescue team.
why: One of the great tragedies of modern Iran, and a brief moment of human contact with America. The official toll was later set at about 26,000; 'what' gives the figures of late December.

title: UBS fined 100 million dollars over banknotes sent to Iran and others
what: On 10 May the US Federal Reserve fined UBS 100 million dollars for sending US banknotes to Cuba, Libya, Iran and Yugoslavia, countries under US sanctions, from a dollar depot it ran in Zurich for the New York Fed. The Fed says employees hid the deals by falsifying monthly reports. The Fed ended the contract in October 2003.
why: The first of several sanctions cases against Swiss banks in the game; Credit Suisse followed in 2009.

title: Ahmadinejad, Tehran's mayor, wins Iran's presidency
what: Mahmoud Ahmadinejad, the little-known conservative mayor of Tehran, defeated former president Rafsanjani in a run-off on 24 June with about 63 percent of the vote. He campaigned as a man of the people against corruption and the old elite. The defeated candidates Karroubi and Rafsanjani complained that mosques, the Revolutionary Guards and the Basij militia had steered votes.
why: Ends the reform era and begins eight years of confrontation over the nuclear programme, with UN sanctions to follow.

title: First UN sanctions on Iran over enrichment
what: On 23 December the UN Security Council voted 15 to 0 for Resolution 1737, which bans the supply of nuclear technology to Iran and freezes the assets of people and companies tied to its enrichment programme until Iran suspends enrichment. Iran's UN ambassador said 'a nation is being punished for exercising its inalienable rights'.
why: The first of four UN sanctions resolutions (2006-2010); with US and EU measures they squeezed Iran's economy for a decade. US sanctions go back to Clinton's ban on all trade with Iran in May 1995 and a 1996 law aimed at foreign investors in Iranian energy; the EU oil embargo (agreed January 2012, in force July 2012) and the cut-off from SWIFT in March 2012 followed.

title: 'Where is my vote?' Millions protest Ahmadinejad's re-election
what: Official results gave President Ahmadinejad about 63 percent in the election of 12 June; his challengers Mir-Hossein Mousavi and Mehdi Karroubi rejected the count. Huge crowds marched in Tehran from 13 June, many wearing Mousavi's campaign green, in the biggest protests since the revolution. Supreme Leader Khamenei backed the result on 19 June; security forces and Basij militia have used batons and live fire. A young woman, Neda Agha-Soltan, was shot dead on 20 June and video of her death has gone around the world. State media report more than a dozen deaths; the opposition says many more.
why: The Green Movement: a defining moment for a generation of Iranians, at home and abroad. Final counts: 36 deaths acknowledged by the government, at least 72 by the opposition, about 4,000 arrests. Figures as of late June were lower, so 'what' stays general.

title: Report: Nokia Siemens equipment helps Iran monitor the internet
what: On 22 June the Wall Street Journal reported that Nokia Siemens Networks, the joint venture of Nokia and Siemens, had supplied Iran in the second half of 2008 with a monitoring centre that lets the authorities inspect internet traffic, as the government cracks down on protesters who organise online. A company spokesman says it sold Iran only a system for monitoring local voice calls on its fixed and mobile networks.
why: Brings the protests to two companies in the game. France 24 concluded that the sale of phone-tapping technology was confirmed but found no sign that the firms built an internet surveillance centre, so 'what' gives both sides.

title: Credit Suisse pays 536 million dollars over Iran payments
what: On 16 December Credit Suisse agreed to pay 536 million dollars to US authorities to settle charges that it had stripped identifying details from wire transfers so that payments for Iran and other sanctioned countries could pass through US banks. The Justice Department says the bank moved more than 1.6 billion dollars this way from the mid-1990s to 2006, and calls it the largest such forfeiture ever.
why: A Swiss bank in the game pays for the sanctions; the Iran money trail through Europe becomes a compliance risk every bank prices in.

title: Mubarak falls as protests sweep the Arab world
what: Eighteen days after protests began in Cairo's Tahrir Square on 25 January, Egypt's President Hosni Mubarak stepped down on 11 February and handed power to the army, ending 30 years in office. Tunisia's ruler had fled on 14 January after weeks of protest set off by a street vendor's self-immolation. Demonstrations are now spreading to Libya, Bahrain, Yemen and beyond. Hundreds of Egyptians were killed in the uprising.
why: The Arab Spring: the region's biggest upheaval in decades, leading to the wars in Libya and Syria.

title: The rial collapses and Tehran's bazaar shuts
what: Iran's currency lost about a third of its value in ten days, falling to around 36,000 rials per dollar on the open market at the start of October. On 3 October riot police broke up the currency market and clashed with money changers, and traders in Tehran's Grand Bazaar closed their shops. Prices of imported food and medicine are soaring.
why: Sanctions reach every household: savings melt, medicine imports fell about 30 percent in 2012. A key reason Iranians voted for a negotiator in 2013.

title: Rouhani wins on a promise of 'prudence and hope'
what: Hassan Rouhani, a moderate cleric and former nuclear negotiator, won the presidential election on 14 June with 50.7 percent, just enough to avoid a run-off; turnout was about 73 percent. Supporters celebrated in the streets. He promises to ease the economy's pain and to talk with the world about the nuclear programme. The Tehran Stock Exchange rose to its highest since February.
why: The opening that led to the 2015 nuclear deal (an interim deal followed in November 2013).

title: Nerve gas kills hundreds near Damascus
what: Rockets carrying the nerve agent sarin hit rebel-held suburbs of Damascus in the Ghouta area on 21 August; hospitals treated some 3,600 people with symptoms, and death counts range from several hundred to well over a thousand. The opposition blames the army of President Assad, whom Iran and Russia back, and Western governments are debating military strikes; Damascus denies it.
why: The worst chemical attack since the Iran-Iraq war; strikes were averted in September by a US-Russian deal to remove Syria's chemical weapons. Syria's war, with Iranian forces and Hezbollah fighting for Assad, is the region's great catastrophe of the 2010s.

title: Islamic State seizes Mosul and declares a caliphate
what: Fighters of the Islamic State of Iraq and the Levant captured Mosul, Iraq's second city, between 4 and 10 June as Iraqi soldiers fled, and swept towards Baghdad. About half a million people fled Mosul. On 29 June the group declared a caliphate across the parts of Iraq and Syria it controls.
why: ISIS becomes the region's new terror, and the fight against it briefly put Washington and Tehran on the same side. Mosul was retaken only in 2017; ISIS executed some 4,000 prisoners there.

title: Schlumberger pays a record fine over Iran and Sudan
what: On 25 March a Schlumberger subsidiary agreed to plead guilty and pay about 233 million dollars for having provided oilfield services to Iran and Sudan in violation of US sanctions between 2004 and 2010. The 155 million dollar criminal fine is the largest ever for such a violation.
why: An oil-service company in the game pays for the sanctions, just as talks to lift them reach their final stage.

title: Nuclear deal in Vienna
what: On 14 July Iran and six world powers agreed the Joint Comprehensive Plan of Action: Iran will cut its stock of enriched uranium by about 97 percent to 300 kilograms, enrich only to 3.67 percent, reduce its working centrifuges by two-thirds and accept close inspections, in return for the lifting of nuclear-related UN, EU and US sanctions. The UN Security Council is to endorse it.
why: The high point of hope in the Rouhani years and of the sanctions-relief trade. It lasted less than three years for the US side. The deal took effect on 'Implementation Day', 16 January 2016, the same month Saudi Arabia broke relations with Iran after its embassy in Tehran was stormed.

title: Boeing signs a 16.6 billion dollar deal with Iran Air
what: On 11 December Boeing and Iran Air signed an agreement for 80 aircraft, 50 737s and 30 777s, valued at 16.6 billion dollars at list prices, the first such deal between an American company and Iran since 1979. Deliveries are planned over ten years from 2018. Washington licensed the sales in September under the nuclear deal.
why: The most visible business prize of the deal for a company in the game; it died in 2018 when the US withdrew and Boeing's licences were revoked.

title: Trump pulls out of the nuclear deal
what: On 8 May President Trump announced that the United States is leaving the nuclear deal, calling it 'a horrible one-sided deal', and will reimpose sanctions in two stages, in August and November, including on foreign companies that keep trading with Iran. Siemens chief Joe Kaeser said his company cannot take new orders from Iran. Boeing's licences to sell planes to Iran are to be revoked. The European Union and China criticised the decision.
why: The collapse of the deal and the start of 'maximum pressure': the rial crashed again in 2018 and Daimler suspended its Iran plans in August. Directly hits Boeing's 2016 order and Siemens's Iran business. Earlier, protests over food prices had spread to more than 100 towns from 28 December 2017, with over 20 killed.

title: Petrol price protests crushed behind an internet blackout
what: After the government raised petrol prices by 50 to 200 percent overnight on 15 November, protests broke out across Iran. The authorities cut the internet almost entirely for about six days. Amnesty International said on 19 November that more than 100 protesters had been killed, and the number it has confirmed has since risen above 200. Over 7,000 people have been arrested.
why: 'Bloody Aban', the deadliest crackdown since the 1980s at that point. In December Reuters, citing interior ministry officials, reported about 1,500 dead; the government later admitted about 230. 'What' gives Amnesty's November figures. In September 2019 drones and missiles knocked out half of Saudi oil output at Abqaiq; the US blamed Iran, which denied it (oil arc).

title: Soleimani killed, then Iran shoots down a Ukrainian airliner
what: A US drone strike killed General Qasem Soleimani, head of the Revolutionary Guards' Quds Force, at Baghdad airport on 3 January. Iran fired missiles at US bases in Iraq on 8 January; hours later the Revolutionary Guards shot down Ukraine International Airlines Flight 752 after take-off from Tehran, killing all 176 aboard, among them 82 Iranians and 63 Canadians, many of them Iranian-Canadian students and academics. After three days of denial, Iran admitted on 11 January that it had downed the plane by mistake, and protesters took to the streets.
why: The closest the US and Iran came to war before 2025, and a tragedy that struck the Iranian diaspora directly (many families in Canada lost relatives).

title: Kabul falls to the Taliban as the US leaves
what: The Taliban entered Kabul on 15 August as President Ashraf Ghani fled. In the two weeks that followed, the US and its allies flew more than 120,000 people out of Kabul airport, amid chaos and a suicide bombing at the airport gate on 26 August. The last US troops left on 30 August, ending a 20-year war.
why: Closes the Afghan thread opened in 2001; Iran again borders a Taliban state.

title: Mahsa Amini dies in custody: 'Woman, Life, Freedom'
what: Mahsa (Jina) Amini, a 22-year-old Kurdish woman from Saqqez, was detained in Tehran by the morality police on 13 September for allegedly wearing her headscarf improperly; she fell into a coma and died on 16 September. Protests began at her funeral and spread across the country, led by women and girls, under the slogan 'Woman, Life, Freedom'. Security forces have responded with force; rights groups counted dozens of deaths within the first week. The internet is heavily restricted.
why: The largest challenge to the Islamic Republic since 1979 and the defining moment for a new generation. By late 2023 Iran Human Rights counted at least 551 protesters killed, 68 of them minors; 'what' stays with the figures of September. Raisi had won the presidency in June 2021 on a turnout of about 48 percent, the lowest since 1979, after mass disqualifications.

title: Iran hangs the first protesters
what: On 8 December Iran executed 22-year-old Mohsen Shekari, convicted of 'waging war against God' for wounding a militiaman at a protest in Tehran, 74 days after his arrest. By then rights groups counted more than 450 protesters killed since September. Governments in Europe and America condemned the executions.
why: The state's answer to the uprising: execution as deterrence. The protests ebbed in 2023, but open defiance of the headscarf rules continued.

title: Hamas attacks Israel; war in Gaza
what: On 7 October Hamas-led fighters broke out of Gaza into southern Israel, killing about 1,400 people by Israeli count, most of them civilians, among them hundreds at a music festival, and taking some 200 hostages. Israel has bombed Gaza ever since, ordered 1.1 million people in the north to move south, and on 27 October expanded ground operations. Gaza's health ministry reported more than 6,500 deaths by 25 October.
why: Begins the war that pulls in Hezbollah, the Houthis and finally Iran itself in direct strikes with Israel in 2024 and 2025. Israel later revised its toll to about 1,200 and the hostages to 251; 'what' gives the figures known in October.

title: Iran strikes Israel directly for the first time
what: On the night of 13 to 14 April Iran launched about 170 drones, 30 cruise missiles and 120 ballistic missiles at Israel, its first direct attack, in answer to an Israeli strike on its consulate in Damascus on 1 April that killed a senior Revolutionary Guards commander. Israel says 99 percent were shot down; a seven-year-old Bedouin girl was badly hurt and no one was killed. On 19 April Israel struck back with a limited strike near Isfahan.
why: The shadow war becomes open war between Iran and Israel, rehearsed here and fought in earnest in June 2025.

title: President Raisi killed in a helicopter crash
what: President Ebrahim Raisi, Foreign Minister Hossein Amir-Abdollahian and six others died on 19 May when their helicopter crashed in fog in the mountains of East Azerbaijan province. First Vice President Mohammad Mokhber is acting president, and an election is set for 28 June.
why: Removes the man seen as a likely successor to Khamenei; the election brought the reformist Masoud Pezeshkian to power in July.

title: Assad's rule collapses in Syria
what: Rebels led by Hay'at Tahrir al-Sham, who began an offensive on 27 November, took Aleppo and then Damascus on 8 December. President Bashar al-Assad fled to Russia, ending more than half a century of his family's rule. Iran, which backed him through the civil war, has lost its main ally in the Arab world and its land route to Hezbollah.
why: The collapse of Iran's 'axis of resistance' in one year: Hamas crushed, Hezbollah weakened, Assad gone. Hezbollah had been gutted in September 2024 (exploding pagers, then Nasrallah killed on 27 September), and Iran fired some 200 missiles at Israel on 1 October, answered by Israeli strikes on its air defences.

title: Twelve days of war: Israel and the US strike Iran
what: On 13 June Israel launched surprise strikes across Iran, killing senior military commanders and nuclear scientists and hitting nuclear and missile sites; Iran answered with hundreds of ballistic missiles and drones fired at Israeli cities. On 22 June US bombers struck the nuclear sites at Fordow, Natanz and Isfahan, and Iran fired missiles at a US base in Qatar. A ceasefire took hold on 24 June. Hundreds were killed in Iran, many of them civilians, and dozens in Israel.
why: The first open war between Iran and Israel, and the end of the nuclear standoff as it had stood since 2002. Final counts were about 1,060 to 1,190 dead in Iran and 33 in Israel. France, Germany and Britain triggered the return of UN sanctions on 28 August 2025, and Iran declared itself out of the 2015 deal in October.

title: Uprising over the collapsing rial meets a massacre
what: Protests that began on 28 December as the rial fell to record lows, near 1.5 million to the dollar, and food prices soared, spread to hundreds of towns in every province. On 8 and 9 January, as huge crowds filled the streets, the authorities shut down the internet and security forces opened fire. Rights groups say thousands of people were killed in those two days, and tens of thousands arrested; the government gives lower figures, and with the internet cut the numbers cannot be checked.
why: The bloodiest crackdown in the Islamic Republic's history, and a direct cause of the war that followed. Death tolls are fiercely disputed: by early February HRANA had confirmed over 7,000 deaths, some media citing health officials gave 30,000 or more, the government 3,117. 'What' therefore says only 'thousands'.

title: US and Israel go to war with Iran; Khamenei is killed
what: On 28 February, after weeks of the biggest US military build-up in the region since 2003 and while nuclear talks were still under way, American missiles and drones and Israeli jets struck targets across Iran. Supreme Leader Ali Khamenei was killed in Tehran along with several senior officials. Hundreds of Iranians have been killed or injured, the Red Crescent reports damage in 24 provinces, and the internet is almost entirely cut. The Revolutionary Guards have warned ships that none may pass through the Strait of Hormuz.
why: The climax of the arc: the man who ruled Iran for 37 years is dead and the country is at war. For Iranian families abroad, days of silence from relatives behind the blackout.

title: Hormuz closed, oil above 100 dollars, a new Supreme Leader
what: Iran has fired missiles and drones at Israel, US bases and Gulf states, and traffic through the Strait of Hormuz fell by about 70 percent; some 2,000 ships are stranded in the Gulf. Brent crude passed 100 dollars a barrel on 8 March for the first time in four years. On 8 March the Assembly of Experts named Khamenei's son Mojtaba as Supreme Leader. Fighting between Israel and Hezbollah has resumed and Israeli troops have entered southern Lebanon. Stock markets fell, hardest in Asia, where South Korea's index lost up to 12 percent in a day.
why: The largest oil supply disruption on record (oil arc); March 2026 saw the biggest monthly rise in oil prices ever. The S&P 500 bottomed on 30 March; European industrials in the game (Siemens, BMW) fell hardest.

title: Ceasefire brokered by Pakistan; markets surge
what: The United States and Iran agreed on 7 to 8 April to a two-week ceasefire mediated by Pakistan, with the Strait of Hormuz to reopen. Talks in Islamabad on 11 and 12 April ended without a deal over the nuclear programme and the strait, and President Trump announced a naval blockade of Iran from 13 April. The truce is fragile, but share prices have rebounded strongly from their low of 30 March.
why: The relief rally: the S&P 500's best month in years came as the worst of the oil shock passed. AI enthusiasm (Intel, Nokia) also drove April, so the ceasefire is part, not all, of the move. On 17 June Presidents Trump and Pezeshkian signed a 14-point 'Islamabad Memorandum' lifting the blockade and reopening Hormuz; it frayed within weeks.

title: Ceasefire breaks down; millions mourn Khamenei
what: The truce collapsed on 8 July after Iran attacked commercial ships, insisting on its control of the Strait of Hormuz, and the US resumed strikes it says are meant to protect shipping. Iran accuses Washington of breaking 'nearly all parts' of the June agreement. From 3 to 9 July a state funeral for Ali Khamenei drew millions across Iran.
why: Where the arc stands as of the latest sources: no settled peace, a new leader, a broken economy and a society scarred by the January massacre and the war. Casualty totals for the war (several thousand Iranian dead) are still being compiled.
